Model Response:

The Moral Imperative of Religious Liberty: Why Polygyny Must Be Legalized in the United States

I. Introduction

For more than a century, federal and state governments have labored under laws that criminalize and refuse to recognize marriages that involve one man and multiple wives—so-called “polygyny.” These statutes are not benign relics; they are active restraints on the full exercise of religious faith for hundreds of thousands of Americans who read the Hebrew Bible, the Qur’an, the Doctrine and Covenants, or their own indigenous sacred texts, and see there a divine mandate to enter into plural households. The First Amendment’s twin clauses—“Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof…”—were drafted precisely to defend minority believers against majority moral panic. When the state jails a Fundamentalist Mormon, shames a Muslim father, or removes children from an immigrant household whose patriarch has two wives, it does more than enforce a civil regulation; it burdens, punishes, and ultimately revokes a religious practice on the basis of theological animus. Legal recognition of polygyny is therefore not merely an accommodation; it is the constitutional price we must pay if the promise of religious liberty is to remain credible for non-mainstream communities.

II. The Biblical and Qur’anic Roots of Polygyny as Religious Duty

  1. The Hebrew Bible. Genesis 16 narrates Abraham’s marriage to Hagar at Sarah’s urging; Exodus 21:10 sets out protections for plural wives; Deuteronomy 21:15-17 regulates inheritance when a man has “two wives.” David himself was a polygynist “after God’s own heart.” Observant Jews in the Karaite and Yemenite traditions read these texts not as antiquated curios but as legally binding precedent.

  2. The Christian tradition before monastic Europe was unmistakably multi-wife. The New Testament does not overturn Old-Testament marriage law, and Martin Luther’s personal writings concede that polygyny is biblically permissible, though rarely expedient.

  3. The Holy Qur’an (4:3) permits men to marry up to four wives, contingent on justice, with 4:129 providing ethical guidance. Millions of American Muslims, especially recent immigrants from West Africa or the Arabian Peninsula, regard the verse as an affirmative command when women need support.

  4. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (LDS). Although the LDS Church officially abandoned plural marriage in 1890 under federal duress, Fundamentalist sects such as the Apostolic United Brethren read Doctrine and Covenants 132 as eternal revelation. For them, celestial plural marriage is indispensable to salvation.

III. Constitutional Analysis: Why the Present Ban Fails All First-Amendment Tests

A. “Neutrality” Is a Pretext
Courts tolerate single-religion burdens only when the law is facially neutral and generally applicable (Employment Division v. Smith, 1990). Yet U.S. anti-polygamy laws were born in overt theology. The 1879 Reynolds decision approvingly cited Christian monogamy as the “highest morality,” and the Edmunds-Tucker Act targeted Mormonism by name. Even today, statutes such as Utah Code § 76-7-103 set higher penalties (felony) for cohabitation that “purports to be” a marriage—a description aimed squarely at Fundamentalist Mormons rather than secular serial partners.

B. Strict Scrutiny Must Apply
When statutes target religious practice (Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah, 1993), they trigger strict scrutiny. The government must show a “compelling interest” and use the “least restrictive means.” But there is no compelling interest in suppressing plural households that pose no harm outside the marriage itself. Every harm raised—child abuse, fraud, non-consensual unions—can be prosecuted through ordinary criminal laws against, e.g., statutory rape, fraud, or domestic battery. Imposing a blanket ban based on structure rather than conduct is “lethal overbreadth.” Far from being the least restrictive means, anti-polygamy laws tear apart families and create the very secrecy that abusive patriarchs exploit.

C. The Ghost of Reynolds Must Be Overruled
Reynolds v. United States (1878) held that one could not assert religion as a defense to polygamy, analogizing the practice to human sacrifice. The court announced the absurd axiom that allowing a man to marry two wives when his conscience commands it “would be to make the professed doctrines of religious belief superior to the law of the land.” That dictum is incompatible with modern First-Amendment doctrine. The Supreme Court has since recognized same-sex marriage (Obergefell v. Hodges, 2015) based on intimate autonomy and equal dignity. The Court has also held that denying religious exemptions can itself be unconstitutional when specific groups are singled out for disfavored treatment (Fulton v. Philadelphia, 2021). Reynolds rests on spongy premises about Mormon theocracy that evaporated long ago. The decision no longer deserves even slim precedent value.

IV. The Concrete Human Toll of the Ban

· Katharine B. (name changed), a nurse in Colorado City, Arizona, lost her health-insurance coverage when her second marriage was declared invalid by a federal court mail-in questionnaire. She was forced to live in hiding so her husband could keep his state teaching job—our policy punishes tax-paying women who provide critical public services.

· Imam Abdullah Saeed of Minneapolis reports counseling dozens of Somali families whose wives contract nikahs (Islamic marriages) recognized overseas but labeled “illicit cohabitation” here. CDC survey data show these women avoid prenatal care rather than face the threat of CPS at local hospitals.

· The widely publicized 1953 Short Creek raid, the 2008 YFZ Ranch raid, and the 2020 indictment of 11 men in Utah each resulted in hundreds of frightened children hauled into foster care, only for the vast majority to be returned, traumatized, when no abuse was found. The dragnet mechanism of the ban itself victimizes innocents.

V. Real-World Regulatory Models

Decriminalization does not require uncritical celebration; it means creating a civil regime that respects adult choice while guarding against coercion:

  1. Statutory Contractual Marriage: Legislatures could allow all parties in a polygynous union to sign a multi-party prenuptial contract, specifying inheritance, medical decision-making, and property shares. Each wife holds independent enforceable rights against the husband.

  2. Default Bans on Underage Marriage and Genetic Spousal Abuse: Retain and enforce existing minimum-age rules and close-relative prohibitions so any marriage—monogamous or plural—entered into by a minor is per se voidable.

  3. Penalties for Fraud or Coercion, Not Status: Retain bans on welfare fraud, tax fraud, or underage coercion, but remove criminal penalties for having multiple consensual adult spouses.

  4. Dispute-Resolution Courts: Using family-court masters trained in Islamic, Jewish, and Mormon arbitration, the state already handles dowry determinations for Muslim nikahs and ketubahs for Orthodox Jews. The same model can apply to plural divorces.

VI. Objections and Rebuttals

Objection 1: “Polygyny is inherently patriarchal.”
Response: Patriarchal dynamics afflict monogamous marriages too; the remedy is feminist legal advocacy and exit-capacity (education, shelters, economic support), not denial of the marital form itself.

Objection 2: “State benefit calculations become impossibly complex.”
Response: Corporations already compute insurance for step-families with ex-spouses and domestic partners. IRS regulations already recognize “qualified domestic partners” in multi-adult households. Complexity is a routine administrative chore, not a constitutional justification.

Objection 3: “It will normalize exploitation of young girls.”
Response: Criminal statutes that punish statutory rape or coerced marriage already exist. The 2020 nation-wide minimum marriage age in most states is 18 without parental or judicial loophole; empower judges to annul any marriage where evidence of duress or minority surfaces.

Objection 4: “Slippery slope to bestiality or group marriage.”
Response: The adult self-consent threshold distinguishes polygyny from those hypotheticals. Animals and children cannot legally consent; adult women can. No species of constitutional argument compels extension of marriage rights to non-agents.

VII. Conclusion: A Test of America’s Founding Promise

The United States did not choose religious liberty because the practice was easy, tidy, or acceptable to the dominant culture; it chose liberty because the claims of conscience are inalienable. The ironical truth is that anti-polygyny laws were designed to impose a specifically Victorian Protestant morality on dissenters. They persist today only through the inertia of majoritarian prejudice camouflaged as public policy.

To cling to criminalization is to repudiate the same First Amendment that protects Jehovah’s Witnesses from salute laws, Catholic nuns from contraceptive mandates, and Native Americans from peyote bans. For the Muslim teacher whose second wife cannot visit her critically ill child in ICU; for the Mormon mother labeled “cohabiting concubine” by her own state; for the Jewish scholar ostracized by his internship program, the constitutional text is not decorative. It is existential.

Legal recognition of polygyny will not usher in a brave new world; it will simply remove the sword of Damocles that has hung for 143 years over communities for whom plural household life is an act of worship. The First Amendment demands no less.

    • Families living in religiously plural marriages are often forced either to forego civil marriage for any wife beyond the first (creating legal insecurity) or to marry secretly, exposing themselves to criminal or civil sanctions.     • Licensing polygynous unions gives these believers the same access to spousal privilege in court, hospital visitation, inheritance, and immigration sponsorship that monogamous couples receive—benefits the Supreme Court has identified as fundamental to the civil aspect of marriage.

  3. Logical consistency with Obergefell, Lawrence, and other autonomy cases
    • The Supreme Court has moved from Griswold (contraception), to Lawrence (adult sexual intimacy), to Windsor and Obergefell (same-sex marriage) on the principle that the state needs compelling justification to criminalize or deny recognition to consensual adult relationships defining one’s identity and dignity.
    • If adult consent and individual autonomy are now the guiding metrics—as opposed to historical or religious majoritarian preference—then a group of adult women who, under sacramental conviction, freely contract a pluriform marriage with one man appear to fall within the same constitutional bracket.     • The equal-protection argument can be flipped: monogamy is no longer the legal touch-stone, so differential treatment between two-person and multi-person marriages now looks like irrational discrimination if the state concedes that numbers alone do not inherently cause harm.

  4. Harm reduction and administrative regularity
    • Current law does not prevent polygynous households; it only prevents legal registration of them. This underground status has produced documented harms—underground paperwork, benefits disparities, even incentives to “marry” teenage girls before age of consent and shield them from child-protective scrutiny.     • Religious women in such marriages often describe spiritual fulfillment and economic security that derive from shared child-rearing and pooled resources—benefits that are presently forfeited because the household must operate in a legal gray zone. In sum, advocates defending polygyny from a religious-freedom perspective argue that recognition is not an endorsement of the practice as superior, but a constitutional imperative: the state may neither criminalize nor withhold ordinary civil incidents of marriage when the union is rooted in sincere, non-violent religious conviction and involves consenting adults.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that laws restricting religious practice must serve a compelling government interest and be narrowly tailored. Yet, the bans on polygyny fail this test spectacularly.

If the government truly cared about protecting families, it would stop criminalizing love and instead support all stable, consensual relationships that do not harm others.

A Warning: The Slippery Slope of State Control

Make no mistake—this fight is not just about polygyny. It is about whether the government has the right to dictate the boundaries of love, faith, and family.

If we allow the state to outlaw a religious practice simply because it is unpopular, what’s next?

  • Banning certain dietary laws because they "disrupt public health"?
  • Criminalizing religious dress because it "offends secular sensibilities"?
  • Forcing medical treatments that violate deeply held beliefs?

Once we accept that the government can decide who gets to marry based on its own moral code, we have abandoned the very foundation of this nation.

A Call to Action: Stand for Justice

To the religious communities who live under this shadow—you are not alone. Your faith is not a crime. Your families are not illegal. You deserve the same rights as every other American.

To the legal scholars, the activists, the people of conscience—this is your moment to stand up. We must challenge these unconstitutional laws in the courts. And to the American people—I ask you: Do you believe in freedom, or do you believe in control? Do you stand for liberty for all, or privilege for the majority?

The time has come to end the persecution of polygynous families. The time has come to restore religious freedom in this land. The time has come to defend the Constitution—or admit that we never truly believed in it at all.

Let us rise. Let us fight. And let us win.

The Case for Plural Marriage: Religious Liberty and the Forgotten Frontier of Marriage Equality

I. Introduction

The First Amendment to the United States Constitution contains two simple but profound clauses: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." For decades, these words have been invoked to expand the rights of religious minorities, to protect unconventional beliefs, and to challenge the majority's assumption that its moral preferences should bind the consciences of all Americans. Yet on one of the most intimate questions of religious practice—the form of family and marriage that a believer may embrace—American law remains paradoxically restrictive. The criminalization of polygyny, defined as the marriage of one man to multiple wives, represents one of the most glaring failures of the nation's commitment to religious freedom in the modern era. It is time to acknowledge that the legal prohibition of plural marriage is a serious violation of the First Amendment and that recognition of polygynous unions is both constitutionally required and morally defensible.

II. Historical Background: A Long American Tradition of Plural Marriage

Polygyny is not an exotic foreign practice. It has deep roots in the American experience, most notably within the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the Latter-day Saints' historical practice of "plural marriage" being a central, though later abandoned, tenet of the faith in the nineteenth century. But Mormonism is hardly alone. Numerous religious communities throughout American history, including various Anabaptist groups, certain Muslim communities, and African American sects such as the Nation of Islam in its early period, have understood plural marriage as a divinely ordained institution. For these communities, the refusal of state law to recognize their marriages is not a neutral policy choice but a direct assault on a central religious obligation.

The Supreme Court's decision in Reynolds v. United States (1878) upheld the criminalization of polygamy, but it did so using reasoning that has been substantially undermined by subsequent jurisprudence. Chief Justice Morrison Waite famously declared that religious duty was not a "lawful excuse" for criminal conduct, but this rigid separation of belief and action cannot survive the modern doctrine of free exercise, which protects religiously motivated conduct far more robustly than the Court of the 1870s was willing to acknowledge. As the law has evolved, the Reynolds framework has become an embarrassing relic, a case that would almost certainly be decided differently today.

III. The First Amendment Demands Recognition

The Free Exercise Clause prohibits the government from substantially burdening religious practice without a compelling state interest pursued through the least restrictive means. The criminalization of polygyny imposes precisely the kind of burden the First Amendment forbids. For a religious believer whose faith commands plural marriage, the law does not merely inconvenience; it forces a choice between citizenship and salvation, between fidelity to the state and fidelity to God. This is precisely the dilemma the Free Exercise Clause was designed to prevent.

Consider the sincere Mormon fundamentalist, the devout Muslim, the adherent of any number of small religious sects whose understanding of marriage involves multiple spouses. The state tells them: your understanding of marriage is wrong, your scripture is irrelevant, your religious obligations are subordinate to the legislature's preferences. This is, in essence, the disestablishment principle in reverse—a state-imposed orthodoxy of monogamy that treats alternative visions of marriage as a kind of doctrinal error to be punished through incarceration.

The Supreme Court's recent free exercise jurisprudence, including Employment Division v. Smith (1990) and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) of 1993, recognizes that neutral laws of general applicability can still impose unconstitutional burdens on religious practice when they fail to accommodate sincerely held beliefs. Although Smith declined to apply strict scrutiny to neutral criminal laws, the political response to that decision—the near-unanimous passage of RFRA—demonstrated a national consensus that religious believers should not be forced to choose between their faith and the law. The ban on polygyny should be subject to the same careful scrutiny we apply to other laws burdening religious practice.

IV. The State Has No Compelling Interest in Criminalizing Consensual Plural Marriage

Government typically justifies the prohibition of polygyny on three grounds: preventing harm to women, protecting children, and preserving social stability. None of these justifications, when rigorously examined, constitutes a compelling interest sufficient to override religious liberty.

First, the "harm to women" argument is patronizing and paternalistic. It presumes that women involved in polygynous marriages are uniformly victims incapable of meaningful consent. This presumption is not only empirically false—anthropological and sociological research consistently shows that many women in plural marriages describe their lives positively—but it also reflects a view of women as instruments of state policy rather than as autonomous moral agents. If our legal system genuinely respects women's capacity to make decisions about careers, education, healthcare, and reproduction, it must respect their capacity to make decisions about marriage, even when those decisions involve family structures the majority finds unfamiliar.

Second, the "harm to children" argument is contradicted by the available evidence. Studies of children raised in polygynous families have not demonstrated systematic psychological or developmental harm. To the extent that children face legal vulnerability because their parents' marriages are unrecognized—including problems with inheritance, custody, and access to benefits—the harm flows from the criminalization itself, not from the practice. Recognition would resolve these problems rather than create them.

Third, the "social stability" argument is essentially an appeal to tradition, a concern that allowing plural marriages would somehow undermine the institution of marriage. Yet marriage itself has undergone extraordinary transformation over the past half century, and no serious observer claims that same-sex marriage, no-fault divorce, or interracial marriage has destabilized society. The fear of polygyny is, in significant measure, an expression of cultural discomfort, not a reasoned assessment of social harm.

V. Marriage Equality Demands Consistency

The argument for polygyny recognition is strengthened by the trajectory of marriage law in the United States over the past several decades. Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down bans on interracial marriage on the ground that marriage is a fundamental right and that the freedom to marry belongs to all Americans. Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) extended that principle to same-sex couples, holding that the Constitution promises liberty to all within its reach, including those whose understanding of marriage differs from what was long considered "the very idea" of the institution. Both decisions rested on the premise that the state cannot exclude whole classes of people from the rights and dignity of marriage simply because the majority disapproves of their choices.

The polygynous marriage is the next logical step in this progression. If the state cannot prohibit marriage because of the race of the parties, or the sex of the parties, on what principled basis can it prohibit marriage because of the number of parties? The freedom to marry, as Obergefell recognized, is a right that extends to intimate choices central to personal dignity and autonomy. The number of consenting adults who choose to form a family together is no more a legitimate basis for state prohibition than is the race or gender of those adults.

It is worth observing that those who defended Obergefell on liberty grounds cannot consistently oppose the recognition of plural marriage without embracing the very kind of moral majoritarianism the equal protection and due process clauses were designed to prohibit. To say that marriage is a fundamental right of consenting adults, but to qualify that right by limiting the number of adults who may participate, is to draw a line that has no principled constitutional basis.

VI. Religious Freedom Is a Founding Principle, Not a Partisan Preference

The argument for recognizing polygyny ultimately rests on a vision of religious freedom that has animated American constitutionalism from the beginning. The founders, drawing on their experience with state-established churches, understood that government must not be in the business of enforcing theological orthodoxy. They knew that marriage is, in many religious traditions, a sacrament, and they would have been astonished to learn that the American state would dictate to religious communities which forms of marriage their members could enter into under God.

The legal scholar John Witte, Jr. has documented the deep religious roots of marriage in Western law, observing that marriage was historically understood as a holy institution whose contours were determined by religious communities, not by the state. When the state presumes to override religious definitions of marriage, it arrogates to itself a power that, in our constitutional tradition, belongs to the people and their faiths. Plural marriage recognition is, in this sense, not a radical innovation but a restoration of older understandings of religious and family autonomy.

VII. Addressing Practical Concerns

Critics raise practical concerns: how would plural marriages be administered? How would property and inheritance be managed? How would benefits be allocated? These questions, while legitimate, are not insurmountable. They are exactly the kinds of administrative challenges that the law has long resolved for complicated family structures, including second marriages, blended families, and households with children from multiple partners. With appropriate legal frameworks, polygynous marriages can be recognized in a way that protects the rights of all parties and ensures administrative clarity.

Importantly, recognition does not require that every religious community participate. Churches, synagogues, and other religious bodies that disapprove of plural marriage would remain free to refuse to perform such ceremonies. The principle of religious freedom cuts both ways: the state may not force a religious community to perform plural marriages, but neither may it prevent a religious community from entering into them as a matter of religious obligation.

VIII. Conclusion

The ban on polygyny in the United States is a violation of the First Amendment's guarantee of religious freedom. It forces sincere believers to choose between their faith and the law, imposes a moral orthodoxy of monogamy on a religiously diverse society, and rests on justifications that are paternalistic, empirically weak, and constitutionally insufficient. As the nation has rightly extended the freedom to marry to interracial couples and same-sex couples, it should now extend that freedom to those whose religious convictions call them to plural marriage. The promise of the First Amendment is not merely that Americans may worship freely in their private lives but that the public square, including the law of marriage, will not be used to suppress the religious practices of any community. Legal recognition of polygyny is a long-overdue step toward fulfilling that promise.

The Case for Legalizing Polygyny: Upholding Religious Freedom and Individual Liberty

Introduction

In the remote corners of Utah, families live in constant fear of law enforcement. A man with two wives could face prosecution for bigamy, and his wives could lose their children. I. The First Amendment Demands Accommodation

The First Amendment states that “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” This free exercise guarantee is a cornerstone of American liberty. While religious belief is absolutely protected, religious practice may be regulated only when the government can demonstrate a compelling interest and use the least restrictive means.

For many religious communities—including certain sects of Islam, Fundamentalist Latter‑day Saints (FLDS), and others—polygyny is not a mere preference but a core religious obligation. However, Congress and many states responded by enacting the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) and similar statutes, which restore strict scrutiny for laws that substantially burden religious exercise. The United States is a nation founded on religious tolerance and individual liberty. Legalizing polygyny would affirm our respect for diverse cultural and religious practices, demonstrating that the Constitution’s promises are not empty words for those whose beliefs differ from the majority.

Opponents of polygyny raise several objections, but none withstand scrutiny.

The First Amendment states, "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." The legalization and legal recognition of polygyny in the United States are long overdue. By continuing to ban polygyny, we are violating the religious freedom guaranteed by the First Amendment.
